entities.label: Movement
entities.summary:
The open source movement, formally launched on February 3, 1998, with the formation of the Open Source Initiative (OSI), fundamentally redefined software development and intellectual property norms. Emerging from the foundational principles of the free software movement championed by Richard Stallman in the 1980s, it sought to promote software licensing models that grant users the freedom to run, study, modify, and distribute software and its source code. This global phenomenon, driven by a diverse community of developers, academics, and corporations, profoundly influenced the architecture of the internet, the evolution of digital infrastructure, and the very philosophy of collaborative innovation in the late 20th and 21st centuries. Key figures like Eric S. Raymond and Bruce Perens, who coined the term 'open source,' aimed to make these practices more palatable to businesses by emphasizing practical benefits over purely ethical concerns.

The genesis of open source can be traced to the late 1990s, when Netscape Communications Corporation, facing market pressure from Microsoft, decided to release the source code for its Communicator browser suite in January 1998, leading to the Mozilla project. This pivotal event, coupled with Raymond’s influential essay 'The Cathedral and the Bazaar' (1997), which articulated the efficiency of distributed, peer-to-peer development, catalyzed the formalization of the movement. The OSI subsequently defined the 'Open Source Definition,' a set of ten criteria for licenses, including free redistribution, access to source code, and permission for derivative works, ensuring broad adoption and standardization across various projects, from operating systems to programming languages.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The open source movement profoundly reshaped the global technological landscape by democratizing software development and fostering a new paradigm of collaborative innovation. It directly enabled the creation of critical internet infrastructure and continues to underpin the vast majority of digital services worldwide.
